goods.timber: White pine for the Royal Navy's masts: the King's broad arrow marked the best trees.
goods.grain: Wheat, rye and Indian corn: the middle colonies were called the bread colonies.
goods.cod: Massachusetts hung a carved wooden cod in its State House. The fish had earned it.
goods.hemp: Parliament paid bounties on colonial hemp, for every ship needed rope by the mile.
goods.sugar_cane: West Indian cane was cut and boiled by enslaved people. The sweetness had a bitter cost.
goods.hides: Cattle hides came by the thousand from Spanish ranchos and backcountry pens.
goods.tobacco: Virginia's cash crop and at times its currency, grown by enslaved and indentured workers.
goods.cotton: Before the gin, picking the seed from a pound of cotton took most of a day's work.
goods.indigo: Carolina indigo, made by enslaved workers over reeking vats, dyed coats blue.
goods.iron_ore: Bog ore dug from swamp bottoms fed the first colonial furnaces.
goods.furs: Beaver felt made Europe's finest hats, and the pelts came through Native hunters.
goods.whale_oil: Train oil lit the lamps of the colonies; sperm oil burned cleaner and sold dearer.
goods.horses: Narragansett Pacers and Chickasaw ponies: the colonies bred a horse for every road.
goods.silver: Silver from Zacatecas and Guanajuato, coined as Spanish dollars, filled colonial purses.
goods.lumber: Sawn boards and barrel staves went by the shipload to the sugar islands.
goods.charcoal: An iron furnace could burn through nearly an acre of woodland in a day.
goods.tar: Tar and pitch sealed every seam and rope in the fleet. The Carolinas made barrels of it.
goods.flour: Philadelphia flour was inspected and branded, and sold from Boston to Barbados.
goods.salt_cod: The best salt cod went to Spain and Portugal; the poorest fed the enslaved in the islands.
goods.rope: Rope was walked, not woven: spinners backed down a long shed paying out hemp.
goods.leather: Tanned for months in oak-bark pits. The smell told you where the tannery was.
goods.molasses: Molasses from the sugar islands was the start of New England's rum trade.
goods.cured_tobacco: Leaf cured brown in the barn, then was prized into hogsheads for inspection.
goods.cloth: Linsey-woolsey: linen one way, wool the other, and warm enough for a hard winter.
goods.candles: Spermaceti candles burned brighter and cleaner than tallow, at a price.
goods.pig_iron: Cast in sand, the ingots lay along the runner like piglets at a sow. Hence the name.
goods.provisions: Barreled beef, pork, bread and peas: a ship's hold was a pantry for months.
goods.sailcloth: Heavy canvas of flax or hemp. A big ship carried yards upon yards of it aloft.
goods.cigars: Israel Putnam is said to have brought Cuban cigars home to Connecticut in 1762.
goods.fur_coats: Beaver, fox and marten, lined and trimmed against a Quebec January.
goods.tools: Axe, hoe and auger: a settler's first purchase and the last thing sold.
goods.barrels: Nearly everything shipped in a cask: flour, fish, rum, nails and tar.
goods.dyed_cloth: Indigo blue, madder red and weld yellow, set fast in the dye-house vats.
goods.saddles: A good saddle outlasted its horse, and sometimes its rider's patience.
goods.silverware: With no banks, colonists turned coin into spoons and tankards they could identify.
goods.rum: Distilled from molasses of slave-worked islands, and traded in turn on the African coast.
goods.muskets: Most colonial muskets came from Britain, and the Brown Bess was the best known.
goods.uniforms: Continental blue faced with buff, whenever the cloth could be found at all.
goods.merchant_ship: Colonial yards built ships cheaply from nearby oak and pine, and sold them in London.
goods.dragoons: Saddle, sword, carbine and boots: everything a mounted soldier needed but the horse.

buildings.lumber: A water-driven saw rose and fell all day, turning logs into boards by the hour.
buildings.charcoal: Colliers tended smoking mounds of wood for days, never letting them burst into flame.
buildings.tar: Pine knots burned slowly under an earth-covered kiln, and the tar ran out below.
buildings.flour: The miller took a toll of every sack, and knew all the news in the county.
buildings.salt_cod: Split, salted and laid out on flakes to dry in the sun and the sea wind.
buildings.rope: A shed some hundreds of yards long, where spinners walked backward twisting yarn.
buildings.leather: Hides soaked for months in pits of oak bark. The neighbors seldom complimented it.
buildings.molasses: Cane juice boiled down through a row of copper kettles, each hotter than the last.
buildings.cured_tobacco: A tall, airy barn where tobacco hung by the stick until it browned.
buildings.cloth: The loom's clack was the steadiest sound in many a colonial house.
buildings.candles: Spermaceti from the whale's head was pressed, refined and molded into fine candles.
buildings.pig_iron: A stone stack fed from the top with ore, charcoal and limestone, blown day and night.
buildings.provisions: Salt beef, hard bread and dried peas, packed in barrels to last a voyage or a campaign.
buildings.sailcloth: Sailmakers sat on long benches with palm and needle, sewing canvas seam by seam.
buildings.cigars: Leaf wrapped around leaf by hand and rolled tight on a wooden board.
buildings.fur_coats: Pelts stretched, scraped and sewn into coats for Montreal winters and London shops.
buildings.tools: Every village wanted a smith: nails, hinges, axes, and a horseshoe while you wait.
buildings.barrels: Staves shaved, bent over a fire and bound with hoops until the cask held water.
buildings.dyed_cloth: Indigo and madder in steaming vats. The dyer's hands stayed blue till Sunday.
buildings.saddles: Leather, wool stuffing and a wooden tree, stitched to fit a horse and a rider.
buildings.silverware: Coin melted and hammered into spoons, porringers and tankards with a maker's mark.
buildings.rum: Molasses fermented in great vats, then ran twice through a copper still.
buildings.muskets: Lock, stock and barrel, fitted by hand, each part filed to fit its own gun.
buildings.uniforms: Coats cut to a pattern and sewn with colored facings, one button at a time.
buildings.merchant_ship: A keel on the stocks, ribs of oak, and half the town turned out for the launch.
buildings.dragoons: Saddlers, armorers and tailors under one roof, fitting out troopers for the field.

gazette: From the Boston Gazette: a ship from Bristol reports fair winds and dear prices for pitch.
The Pennsylvania Gazette notes flour plentiful at the wharves and buyers holding out for less.
From the Virginia Gazette: the tobacco warehouses at the falls are full, and inspectors busy.
The New-York Gazette reports a sloop in from Jamaica with molasses, limes and a lame parrot.
From the Maryland Gazette: a runaway horse, bay, found in a cornfield. The owner may apply.
The South-Carolina Gazette reports rice and indigo in good demand at Charles Town.
From the Boston News-Letter: the harbor froze early this year, and the fish are dearer for it.
La Gazette de Québec reports the fur canoes safe down from the upper country.
La Gaceta de México reports the silver trains arrived at the capital without mishap.
The Pennsylvania Gazette advertises spermaceti candles, fresh from Newport, at the sign of the Ship.
From the Virginia Gazette: a dry summer. Planters look to the sky and the price of corn.
The Boston Gazette reports cod scarce on the near banks; the schooners go farther out.
From the New-York Gazette: salt is short, and every fisherman in the port has noticed.
The Maryland Gazette notes a new ferry at the narrows, with a boat that seldom sinks.
From the South-Carolina Gazette: a hurricane passed to the south, sparing the harbor.
The Pennsylvania Gazette reports German wagoners in town with butter, hides and opinions.
From the Boston Gazette: a whaler home from a long voyage, full to the hatches with oil.
The Virginia Gazette advertises a stallion standing at stud, of fine blood and fair temper.
La Gazette de Québec notes the ice going out of the river, and the first ship expected soon.
From the New-York Gazette: London prices for beaver are up, and the traders are smiling.
The Boston News-Letter reports a snow so deep the post rider arrived three days late.
From the Pennsylvania Gazette: a new printing of the almanac, with tides and good advice.
The Maryland Gazette notes iron from the upriver furnaces coming down by the boatload.
From the South-Carolina Gazette: naval stores in demand; tar and turpentine fetch good prices.
La Gaceta de México notes a good harvest in the Bajío and bread cheaper in the city.
The New-York Gazette reports a packet boat in from Falmouth with letters and little else.
From the Boston Gazette: a lottery is proposed to pave the street by the town dock.
The Virginia Gazette reports hemp coming on well in the upper valley this season.
From the Pennsylvania Gazette: rum and sugar steady, cloth dearer, and news from Europe old.
The Boston News-Letter notes a fair wind from the east and every ship in the harbor making sail.
founding: Axes ring in the clearing; the first chimney smokes by nightfall.
A cart, a cow, a crate of seed, and a great deal of optimism.
The first cabin goes up crooked. Nobody minds; it keeps the rain out.
Someone plants an apple tree. It's a promise to stay.
The surveyor's chain is barely stowed before the first fence is argued over.
A clearing, a spring, and a view worth the walk. The settlers unload.
The wagons are unhitched, and for the first time in weeks nobody is going anywhere.
By the first evening there is a fire, a pot of stew, and a name for the place.
The first well is dug. The water is cold, clear, and a matter of great local pride.
A signpost goes up at the crossroads, pointing proudly at the woods.
The children have already found the creek. The adults find the mosquitoes.
A bell is hung from a tree limb, for church, for dinner, and for fire.
The first letter home is written by candlelight: 'Come in the spring.'
Stumps in the fields, smoke in the chimney, and a new mark on the map.
The first harvest is a long way off, but the first loaf of bread is tonight.
